F2.Q1: Dry-laid sandstone flagging — flat tan slabs in irregular courses, set with dark joints. No mortar bed visible; the joints read as gaps, not fill.
F2.Q1_WHY: The colour is one narrow tan family everywhere (sampled across the lit core, R:G:B holds at roughly 1 : 0.75 : 0.42 with no hue departures anywhere). The pieces are cut rectangles in mixed sizes — big ones around 50×37px next to small ones around 25×18px (clearly visible x 280–360, y 150–200) — laid in rough courses with staggered vertical joints. That is flagging, not brick, not tile, not cast slab. But I am naming the material from silhouette and colour alone. Nothing on the face of any stone tells me it is sandstone rather than limestone, concrete, or painted board. There is no grain, no bedding, no grit.
F2.Q2:
South, down the corridor at x 375–438.

Nothing about the ground influenced that. I picked it because the walls pinch in on both sides at x≈375 and x≈440 and form a channel — that is a wall read, not a floor read. The ground inside the corridor mouth (x 380–435, y 275–330) is the identical stone at the identical tone, with the identical joint rhythm and the identical crack line-work as the room floor I am standing on. If you deleted the walls I would have no reason to go south rather than north.
F2.Q3:
It has been cracked, thoroughly and evenly, and nothing else has ever happened to it.

There are long fracture lines running everywhere and about a dozen dark spiky blotches scattered across it. But it has not been *used*. There is no wear. No polish, no dishing, no scuffing, no dirt in the low corners, no grime banked against the wall bases, no darkening at the corridor threshold, no chipped arrises on the stones nearest the doorway. Nothing has been dragged across it, dropped on it, spilled on it or repaired on it — no rope, no pins, no patch timber, no salvaged stone set in at a wrong angle. For a place in continuous heavy use since before the records, the ground is unmarked by traffic.
F2.Q3_WHY:
I flattened the lamp falloff out (fitted brightness against radius from the figure at ~410,178 and divided it out) and looked at what albedo is left underneath. The answer is: essentially none. Across 291 sampled stone-face interiors inside the lit core, residual albedo std is 0.14, and most of that is my own model error at the edges. Every stone face is the same value as every other stone face. The one exception in the whole image is a single large dark slab at x 525–600, y 82–112 — and it sits out in the gloom where it barely registers.

The cracks also don't behave like damage. Follow the long one that enters at about (300, 215) and runs up-right to (410, 185): it crosses a stone joint at x≈304 and continues through with no deflection, no offset, no step. It holds a constant 1px width for its entire run and has no spalling, no chipped edge, no lighter freshly-broken interior, no dark depth to the void. It is a line lying on top of the stones, not a break in them.
F2.Q4:
Yes — the spiky starburst blotch. About twelve of them, at roughly (217,35), (340,33), (402,60), (585,60), (400,102), (342,170), (612,170), (270,228), (420,235), (472,242), (590,232), (535,260).

Every one is the same motif: a dark irregular disc about 20–25px across with short spikes radiating off the rim, some filled, some open in the middle like a ring. They are all the same size, all the same value, and they are spread at a suspiciously even pitch — roughly 110px apart in every direction, including out in the dark where I am told not to look and where no one will ever see them.

I checked whether they are literally the same stamp. They are not: cross-correlating the eight clearest against each other under all four rotations and both mirrors, nothing exceeded 0.35. They are individually drawn. It doesn't help. They are individually drawn *variations on one idea*, applied at constant density, and my eye finds them faster than it finds the room.

Second thing, smaller: the diagonal hatch. Short parallel dashes at 45° on stone faces at x 520–620 / y 120–220 and along the top band x 190–420 / y 0–60. It only ever appears on dim stones. Inside the lamp there is none. Which tells me the hatch is doing shading work, not material work — it's a dither, dressed as texture.
F2.Q5:
An image that was repeated — with one real exception.

The exception is the layout, and I want to credit it properly because I went looking to fail it. There is no tiling here. Autocorrelating the floor band horizontally and vertically from 4px to 80px produces a flat monotonic curve with no periodic minimum — no grid repeat at any scale I tested. Normalising 25px blocks and comparing all pairs, the best matches (0.247, 0.338) are all pairs of *blank* faces matching each other, and the population median is 1.124. The stonework genuinely does not repeat. Someone laid this out.

But the layout is the only made thing. The surface on top of it is three marks — crack polyline, starburst blotch, diagonal hatch — scattered at uniform density over the entire floor, corner to corner, lit and unlit alike, with no regard for where anything is. A floor that was made would have a story in the distribution: more damage where the load is, dirt where it collects, nothing where nothing happens. This has the same event rate everywhere. That is a scatter pass, not a history.
F2.Q6:
YES. It is clean, coherent, correctly lit, readable at size, and the stonework layout is above average for the category.

Merely competent. Not good. The non-repeating layout is real craft, and it is spent on a surface with nothing on it. The floor is a diagram of a floor: correct plan, empty faces.
F2.Q7:
Legible at 1:1, on the floor: the joint grid; the long crack polylines; the dark blotches; the lamp falloff. That is the complete list — and note that all four are *outline and value*. Not one of them is the face of the material.

**The faces are blank at 1:1.** Flat unmodulated tan. Not "subtle" — absent.

Only on magnification: the 45° hatch dashes on the dim stones; a few small rectangular inset marks in the top band; and an extremely faint per-stone tonal blocking. I had to hunt for all of it, and the hatch isn't material anyway, it's shading.
F2.Q7_WHY:
Checked at 1:1 (from the unmagnified 750×600 view): x 280–360 / y 150–200 (open faces just left of the figure) — blank. x 200–260 / y 120–260 (the wide lit stones on the left) — blank. x 440–520 / y 140–230 (right of the figure) — blank. x 380–435 / y 275–330 (corridor mouth) — blank. The corridor interior x 375–438 / y 275–480 — blank.

Had to magnify (4×–8×): x 520–620 / y 120–220 to find the hatch. x 190–420 / y 0–60 to find the dashes and inset marks. x 280–360 / y 150–200 at 8× to confirm the faces really are empty and not just low-contrast — they are empty.

The measurement, on eroded face interiors only with joints and cracks excluded: high-pass std is 3.9 against a mean of 164 in the lit core. 2.4% relative contrast. On a phone that is nothing. Out in the dim ring it reaches 4.9% relative, but the absolute signal there is ~3 levels. Whatever texture exists is below the threshold where the medium can carry it.
F2.Q8:
It reads as one age everywhere, and the age it reads is contradictory: **laid last year and then hit once, hard, all over.**

The crack density says centuries. The faces say the stone came out of the yard this morning. Those two can't both be true, and the absence wins the argument — cracking is cheap to fake and wear is not, so a floor with cracks and no wear reads younger than a floor with wear and no cracks. My honest number: a decade of standing, one afternoon of damage, zero years of traffic.

Nothing distinguishes any part of it. Not one region is older or newer than another. The floor by the wall (x 190–230) is the same age as the floor at the doorway (x 380–435, y 260–290) is the same age as the floor under the lamp. In a place that has been administered continuously since before the records, with a company holding a line on it for four hundred years, there is no second generation of stone anywhere — no patch, no replacement, no re-set slab, no repair of any kind.
F2.Q8_WHY: Crack evidence from x 245–410 / y 180–220 and x 200–380 / y 30–130. Absence-of-wear evidence from the flattened-albedo pass over the whole lit floor x 185–620 / y 0–270 — uniform. Threshold evidence from x 360–460 / y 260–290: the stone runs through the doorway unchanged, no darkening, no rounded edges, no threshold slab. Wall-base evidence from x 185–210 / y 100–260 and x 600–620 / y 100–260: no accumulation, no grime, no debris where the floor meets the wall.
F2.Q9:
No. The ground told me nothing. I read the route off the walls.

There is a route — south, down the channel at x 375–438, and north where the room runs off the top edge — but I know that because the walls close in, not because the floor says so.
F2.Q9_WHY:
Along the south route I checked x 380–435 at y 275–300, 300–330, and 330–360. Against the rejected directions: x 200–300 / y 150–250 (west), x 500–600 / y 150–250 (east), x 250–550 / y 0–60 (north). The difference between the route and the rejections is zero. Same stone, same joint pitch, same crack vocabulary, same tone once the lamp is divided out, same blotch density. The stone in the corridor at (400, 300) is indistinguishable from the stone in the dead west corner at (220, 200).

What a walked route would have and this doesn't: a centre line worn lighter or darker than its margins, edges of the traffic lane where dirt banks up, stones dished in the middle of the channel, the corridor mouth scuffed where four hundred years of shoulders have turned the corner. There is none of it. I am told I am standing on ground that is walked daily and I cannot find the path under my own feet.
F2.Q10:
They all look the same.

There are two openings in view: the corridor mouth south at x 375–438, y ≈272, and the room continuing north off the top edge across x 217–554, y = 0. The ground immediately inside each is identical in tone, joint pattern and mark density. Nothing marks one as the road and the other as the door nobody opens. In a filing system for souls, in continuous heavy use, with a garrison holding one line, the floor should be shouting which way everyone goes. It is silent.
F2.CULL: Stone faces are blank — every mark is outline; the material itself has no surface at 1:1.
F2.FLIP LIST:
- Put material on the faces: grit, bedding, pitting and colour break-up on the stone interiors, at contrast that survives at 1:1 (target ≥8% local, vs the 2.4% measured now at x 280–360 / y 150–200).
- Vary albedo stone to stone. Right now 291 sampled faces come back at one value; give the flagging a distribution of tone, weathering and cut quality so no two neighbours match.
- Cut the starburst blotch count by two thirds and stop scattering it evenly. Remove those at (585,60), (612,170), (590,232), (535,260); keep clusters where something plausibly happened.
- Make the cracks behave: deflect or step them at every joint they meet, vary the width, and spall the edges — the run through (300,215)→(410,185) currently crosses a joint at x≈304 with no offset and holds one pixel of width throughout.
- Build wear into the route: a darker, dished traffic lane down the corridor at x 375–438, dirt banked at the wall bases (x 185–210, x 600–620), and scuffed rounded stone at the doorway threshold (x 360–460, y 260–290) — with the north opening deliberately left clean so the two read differently.

F1.Q1: Cut stone flagging — irregular rectangular slabs, dry-laid, no mortar bed, sizes all over the place. Sandstone or a pale limestone.
F1.Q1_WHY:
The slab layout does the work. I segmented 123 slab faces between x=183–618, y=0–268 and got 103 distinct sizes — a running bond that never settles into a course. Compare x=371–427, y=115–143 (one long slab, 56px) against x=475–489, y=147–165 (a 14px offcut two rows down). That's stone cut to fit a hole, not tile. Joints are a 1–2px dark line with a stippled, uneven edge rather than a clean rule — the slabs don't meet squarely. Colour sits in the tan/ochre band (RGB roughly 200/165/115 at the brightest, x=452–486 y=138–158), which reads as a pale sedimentary stone, and it is the same material everywhere including down the corridor.

---
F1.Q2:
South, down the corridor at x=375–440.

But I have to split the answer, because the honest version is uncomfortable: **the shape of the ground picked it, the surface of the ground told me nothing.** The lit floor narrows into a two-slab-wide channel at y=270 and runs down to about y=416 where the lamp gives out. That's an unambiguous route and it's the only one fully inside the light. Everything else — north across the top of the frame, east past x=560, west past x=250 — is a wide open floor edge that just gets dark.

What did *not* influence me: any mark on the surface. There is no worn line, no polish, no scatter of grit pushed to the sides, nothing on the slab faces at x=375–440, y=280–400 that says people go this way. If you flipped the corridor to the north side of the room and left the surface untouched, I would have made the same choice for the same reason and noticed nothing missing.

---
F1.Q3:
Two things, and they are happening in different places.

It has cracked, comprehensively. A network of thin dark fissures runs across the whole lit chamber, ignoring the joints entirely — they cut *through* slab faces and carry on into the next one. And separately, a large number of slabs are carved: blocks of short horizontal dashes stacked in rows, like lines of writing, plus fields of diagonal hatching and small scratch patches.

The problem is that nothing has happened to the floor **you can actually see**. The carved slabs are all out at the dim edges. The lit floor — the ground the figure is standing on — is unmarked. Not lightly marked. Unmarked.
F1.Q3_WHY:
The cracks I can point at directly: a long diagonal enters around x=230, y=45, runs down-right and passes clean through the slab at x=305–337, y=147–165 without deflecting at either joint; another crosses the frame left-to-right at y≈220–240 from x=190 to x=470. They cross slab boundaries, which is why they read as fracture rather than as a drawn edge.

The carving is at x=505–618 across all y, at x=185–340 y=0–110, and along the top rows y=0–45. Magnify x=400–620, y=0–140 and you find dash-rows on nearly every face — the slab at x=555–600, y=95–115 has four stacked rows of them.

Now magnify x=330–500, y=110–250, the lamp-lit centre. Flat fill, a soft vertical gradient, one crack. Nothing else. I normalised for lighting (divide by a 10px Gaussian, so brightness can't hide anything) and measured per-slab detail energy on 114 slabs with the sprite excluded: slabs at mean brightness 100–200 average **0.128**; slabs at brightness 0–70 average **0.157–0.177**. The best-lit third of the floor is objectively the emptiest third. The lamp is not washing detail out — the detail was never placed there.

---
F1.Q4:
Yes, two things.

**The hard vertical seam at x≈500–508, running y=140–260.** My eye goes back to it every pass. To its left, the slabs are blank tan. To its right, every single slab carries hatching or dash-rows. The material changes character across a straight vertical line that isn't a joint, isn't a crack, and isn't anything in the layout. It's a lighting boundary, and the floor's entire surface vocabulary is switching on and off with it. Once you see it you can't stop seeing it — it makes the lit floor look like a hole cut in a different, better floor.

**The stair-stepped shadow edge at x≈240–260, y=155–250**, left of the figure. Same effect, mirrored: hard diagonal boundary, blank slabs on the lit side, carved slabs immediately across it at x=195–235, y=170–210.

Together they frame the player in a rectangle of empty ground roughly x=255–505, y=110–250, with all the interesting material pushed outside it.

---
F1.Q5:
**Made.** This one is genuinely earned.

I autocorrelated the lighting-normalized chamber looking for a stamp period — nothing. No local maximum anywhere in offsets up to dy=150/dx=200; the correlation decays monotonically and the only elevated values are the horizontal joint banding, which is what slab courses are *supposed* to produce. I then compared every same-size slab pair for identical content. The closest matches came in at diff=0.089–0.13, and when I looked at which slabs those were — x=431–455/y=253–268 against x=373–397/y=253–268 — they match because they are both **blank**. Two empty slabs are identical for a boring reason.

So: no stamped grid, no duplicated marks, no tiling seam. The layout was authored. Credit where it's due. It just doesn't rescue the rest.

---
F1.Q6:
**YES.** It is coherent, it is not obviously broken, it would pass in a screenshot.

Merely competent, or genuinely good? **Merely competent.** The slab layout is good work. The surface treatment is not, because the surface treatment is invisible in the one place the player is looking. Good means the material rewards attention at the size it's played at. This one punishes it — you look at the ground under your feet and there is nothing there.

---
F1.Q7:
Legible at 1:1, on the face of the material:
- The crack network. That's it. Thin dark lines, high contrast against the lit tan, clearly readable.

Also legible at 1:1 but not surface: the joints, the slab sizes, the light falloff.

**Not legible at 1:1 — only appears on magnification:**
- The dash-row carvings. All of them.
- The diagonal hatch fields.
- The small scratch and pitting patches.
- Any grain or tonal variation within a slab face.

**At 1:1, under the lamp, the faces are blank.** I want to be plain about that: the region x=255–505, y=110–250 has no legible surface content whatsoever except cracks. In the dark regions there is *something* — you can tell the slabs aren't flat — but it reads as undifferentiated noise, not as marks, and it's too dark to resolve.

And the carvings are the best idea in this floor. Rows of short parallel dashes stacked in blocks, on the ground of a place that files souls — that's the fiction sitting right there on the stone. The player never sees it. I only found it by dividing the image by a Gaussian blur. That is hunting, not seeing.
F1.Q7_WHY:
- **Checked at 1:1** (the unmagnified 750×600 read): x=330–500 y=110–250 (lamp centre); x=180–620 y=0–270 (whole chamber); x=375–440 y=270–420 (corridor). Cracks read. Faces do not.
- **Had to magnify** (4×–6× nearest-neighbour, plus lighting normalisation to see anything at all): x=400–620 y=0–140 — dash-rows and hatching on nearly every slab; x=180–400 y=0–140 — same; x=505–618 y=140–270 — heaviest carving in the image; x=190–260 y=155–250 — carved slabs on the shadowed side of the stair-step edge. Every one of these needed magnification. Several needed magnification *and* a brightness fix.

---
F1.Q8:
It reads as **two different ages in one room**, and the boundary between them is a lighting edge, which is the tell that this is a production artifact rather than a story.

**The dim floor: older than the records.** x=505–618 (all y), x=185–340 (y=0–110), and the top rows y=0–45. Slabs carved over and over — the dash-rows at x=555–600 y=95–115 and x=490–545 y=10–35 are stacked in multiple passes at different densities, which reads as accumulation over a long time rather than one event. Fractures crossing many slabs at once mean the whole bed has moved, and that takes settlement, not an accident.

**The lit floor: laid last week.** x=255–505, y=110–250. Blank, uniform, uncarved, unworn. The slab at x=371–427 y=115–143 is a large clean face directly north of the figure with a single crack across it and nothing else. If I saw only that region I would say this floor is new.

The two ages meet at x≈500 on a straight vertical line and at the stair-step around x≈250. Neither boundary corresponds to a repair seam, a different stone, a joint run, or anything a mason would have done. The floor gets four centuries older exactly where the lamp stops reaching. That's the failure stated as an age reading.
F1.Q9:
It goes **south**, down the channel at x=375–440 to about y=416 where the light dies.

**I read it off the walls and off the shape of the lit area — the ground surface told me nothing.** I want that recorded clearly, because the question is asking whether ground that is walked daily looks walked, and the answer is no. The corridor floor is the blankest ground in the image.
F1.Q9_WHY:
- **Route, accepted:** x=375–440, y=270–420. Slab faces here at (373–397, 253–268) and (401–427, 253–268) rank among the fourteen emptiest in the whole image — detail energy 0.051 and 0.038 against a chamber mean of 0.15. Magnified (my corridor crop, x=370–460 y=270–470), it is a clean running bond, flat fills, one hairline joint offset near y=310. No polish down the centre. No grit pushed to the walls. No dishing where feet land. Nothing that separates the middle of the walkway from the edges.
- **Rejected, north** (x=311–540 at y=0, where floor still reaches the top of frame): rejected only because it exits the frame with no visible destination. The ground there is *more* marked than the corridor, not less — carved slabs across y=0–45. If I were reading traffic off the surface, the carving would argue people go north, which is the opposite of what the layout says.
- **Rejected, east and west** (x>560, x<250 at mid-height): rejected because the floor edge dissolves into shadow with no channel forming.
- **What is different about the ground between them:** in terms of surface, nothing that indicates use. The corridor is emptier than the chamber, and the chamber is emptier under the lamp than at its dark edges. The gradient of detail in this image tracks illumination, not footfall. There is no traffic signal on this floor at any point.

---
F1.Q10:
**They all look the same.**

Two openings are readable: the north continuation across the top of the frame (floor still present at y=0, x≈311–540) and the south corridor mouth at x=375–440, y=268–290. I compared the ground immediately in front of each. The corridor mouth slabs at (373–397, 253–268) and (401–427, 253–268) measure 0.051 and 0.038 detail energy. The chamber floor either side of the mouth — (283–303, 169–207) at 0.041, (433–449, 175–207) at 0.032 — measures the same. There is no darkening, no wear fan, no scuff spreading out from the threshold, nothing accumulating in the corners where nobody walks.

If one of these is the door a company of soldiers has used every day for four hundred years and the other is bricked-up dead ground, the floor does not know which is which.

---
